name: Sciatica
definition: Pain, and sometimes tingling, numbness or weakness, in one leg when the sciatic nerve is irritated or compressed.
overview: Sciatica describes symptoms that arise when the sciatic nerve, which runs from the lower back to the feet, is irritated or compressed. The NHS lists pain, tingling, numbness or weakness in one leg, often worse with movement, sneezing or coughing. A slipped disc is the most common cause. The NHS says recovery usually takes from a few weeks to a few months, though it can take longer and sciatica may return. Numbness around the genitals or bottom, or problems controlling the bladder or bowels, need an emergency response.
causes: Slipped (herniated) disc pressing on a nerve root, the most common cause
Spinal stenosis, a narrowing of the spaces in the spine
Spondylolisthesis, where a bone in the spine slips out of position
riskFactors: Regular lifting and other physical stress on the spine
Whole-body vibration, for example in some jobs
signs: Leg pain on one side that is more severe than any back pain, often running below the knee
Tingling or numbness in the lower leg
complications: Symptoms that last longer than a few months or come back
Cauda equina syndrome, a rare but serious emergency involving the nerves at the bottom of the spinal canal
Persistent symptoms that lead to referral for injections or surgery
diagnosis: Sciatica is mainly diagnosed from the person's history and a physical examination. One review notes that there is no single specific test, so clinicians use several examinations and also look for red flag features such as cancer, fracture and cauda equina syndrome. NICE advises against routinely offering imaging in a non-specialist setting and suggests considering imaging in specialist settings only if the result is likely to change management.
treatment: The NHS lists exercises, painkillers and physiotherapy as the main treatments. NICE puts self-management and information about the condition at the centre of care. In severe cases the NHS says people may be referred for procedures such as epidural injections or decompression surgery.
prevention: A review of risk factors notes that some, such as whole-body vibration and strenuous physical activity at work, may be modifiable. The NHS says sciatica may come back.
seekCare: Call 999 or go to A&E for sciatica on both sides, worsening leg weakness or numbness, numbness around the genitals or bottom, or problems controlling the bladder or bowels; the NHS advises against driving yourself. Pain that is not settling after several weeks is a reason for a GP appointment, because specialist referral is considered when symptoms do not improve with conservative treatment.

sections.heading: What is sciatica and what does it feel like?
sections.body:
Sciatica is the name given to symptoms that arise when the sciatic nerve is irritated or compressed. This nerve runs from the lower back down to the feet. The NHS describes the symptoms as pain, tingling, numbness or weakness in one leg, which are often worse with movement, sneezing or coughing.

A medical review describes the typical picture as pain in one leg that is more severe than any back pain, often running below the knee, with tingling or numbness in the lower leg. Versus Arthritis describes the pain as travelling from the back or buttock down the leg towards the foot. The NHS also says that back pain on its own is not usually sciatica.

sections.heading: What causes sciatica?
sections.body:
The NHS says a slipped disc is the most common cause of sciatica. Versus Arthritis explains that in this case a disc in the back bulges and presses on a nerve, squeezing and irritating a nerve root. A medical review likewise says sciatica is usually caused by irritation of a nerve root, most often from a herniated lumbar disc.

Other causes listed by the NHS are spinal stenosis, spondylolisthesis and an injury to the back. Spinal stenosis is a narrowing of the spaces in the spine, and spondylolisthesis is when one bone in the spine slips out of position. One review also lists infection, inflammation, tumours and blood vessel disease among possible causes that do not start in the spine. Reviews of risk factors mention age, regular lifting, whole-body vibration, smoking, obesity and psychological stress.

sections.heading: How is sciatica diagnosed?
sections.body:
Sciatica is mainly diagnosed from the person's history and a physical examination. One review notes that there is no single specific test for sciatica, so clinicians use several examinations. The straight leg raise is described as the most common test, although its accuracy is mixed. Doctors also check for red flag features of other problems, such as cancer, fracture and cauda equina syndrome.

NICE advises against routinely offering imaging in a non-specialist setting. It suggests considering imaging in specialist settings only if the result is likely to change management. NICE also says a risk stratification tool, such as the STarT Back tool, can be considered at first contact to guide shared decisions about care. For suspected cauda equina syndrome, one regional spinal network policy says MRI is the only way to confirm it.

sections.heading: How is sciatica treated?
sections.body:
The NHS lists exercises, painkillers and physiotherapy as the main treatments. A medical review describes initial treatment as conservative, with education, advice to stay active and continue daily activities, and adequate pain relief. NICE puts self-management and information about the condition at the centre of care. Versus Arthritis notes that a physiotherapist can help recommend an exercise programme.

The NHS says paracetamol is unlikely to help and that it is unclear how much anti-inflammatory painkillers such as ibuprofen help. NICE does not recommend gabapentinoids for sciatica and advises against offering oral corticosteroids or benzodiazepines for it. It also advises against opioids for chronic sciatica, and against belts or corsets, foot orthotics, traction and ultrasound.

sections.heading: How long does sciatica last, and what if it does not settle?
sections.body:
The NHS says recovery usually takes from a few weeks to a few months, though it can take longer and sciatica may return. The NHS suggests staying active, doing regular sciatica exercises and using heat packs on the painful area. NHS hospital self-care advice says there is no single best exercise for sciatica, so choosing activities that a person enjoys is reasonable. A medical review recommends continuing daily activities rather than stopping them.

For severe cases, the NHS says people may be referred for procedures such as epidural injections or decompression surgery. Versus Arthritis says injections are sometimes used for severe sciatica when other treatments have not worked, and that an operation is sometimes needed to free the nerve. A medical review says referral to a specialist is generally considered when symptoms do not improve after several weeks of conservative treatment. A trial protocol notes that epidural injections have only a small short-term effect on leg pain and disability compared with placebo.

sections.heading: When is sciatica an emergency?
sections.body:
The NHS says sciatica on both sides, worsening weakness or numbness in the leg, numbness around the genitals or bottom, and problems controlling the bladder or bowels need urgent attention. The NHS route is an A&E visit or a call to 999, and it advises against driving yourself. Clinical literature describes cauda equina syndrome as a rare but serious complication in which the nerve bundle at the bottom of the spinal canal is compressed. Its features include difficulty passing urine, numbness in the saddle area around the perineum, pain in both legs, weakness, and bowel or bladder control problems.

Surgical decompression is described as the effective treatment. A UK patient leaflet says outcomes are better especially when treatment starts within 24 hours of the symptoms beginning. Leg pain that is not improving is a different situation, and a GP appointment is the usual route for discussing it.

faqs.q: How long does sciatica take to get better?
faqs.a: The NHS says recovery usually takes from a few weeks to a few months, although it can take longer and sciatica may come back. Exercises, painkillers and physiotherapy are listed as the main treatments. A GP appointment is the usual route for discussing symptoms that are not improving, and severe cases may be referred for procedures such as epidural injections or decompression surgery.

faqs.q: Is sciatica the same as a slipped disc?
faqs.a: They are linked but not identical. Sciatica describes the symptoms of an irritated or compressed sciatic nerve, and the NHS says a slipped disc is the most common cause. Versus Arthritis describes a slipped disc as a disc in the back that bulges and presses on a nerve. Other causes include spinal stenosis, spondylolisthesis and back injury.

faqs.q: Is it better to rest or stay active with sciatica?
faqs.a: The NHS suggests staying active, doing regular sciatica exercises and using heat packs on the painful area. Versus Arthritis calls staying active the most important way people can help themselves with back pain. A physiotherapist can help recommend an exercise programme.

faqs.q: Do I need an MRI scan for sciatica?
faqs.a: Sciatica is mainly diagnosed from a person's history and a physical examination. NICE advises against routinely offering imaging in a non-specialist setting and suggests imaging in specialist settings only when the result is likely to change management. A scan may be used if cauda equina syndrome is suspected.

The NHS says sciatica on both sides, worsening leg weakness or numbness, numbness around the genitals or bottom, and bladder or bowel control problems need an A&E visit or a call to 999. It advises against driving yourself. These can be features of cauda equina syndrome, a rare but serious condition.
